Header:
Date: 2025-03-11
Start: 09:30 AM PT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Product), Ethan Zhou (Redwood SRE); Samir Shah (CTO), Lena Ortiz (SRE), Marcus Lee (ML Eng), Rina Gomez (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, optional): mid-sized technical deep dive on autoscaling design for mixed inference workloads. Key themes: burst policy design, queueing models, reserved vs burst GPUs, cold-starts and model load time, batching and KV cache strategy, quantization tradeoffs for latency. Action items around traces, cost model, and benchmark runway.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we've got about 75 minutes blocked, want to make sure we focus on the capacity and autoscaling architecture and leave time for questions. Quick intros?
[00:12] Samir Shah: Samir here, CTO at Polaris. Long story short — we have a prod gen AI feature in our triage pipeline, roughly 1.2M requests/day but very spiky from telemedicine bursts. We're worried about p95 latency during bursts, and also the cost of overprovisioning GPUs.
[00:28] Daniel Park: Thanks, Samir. I'm Daniel, SE. We ran a quick read of your shared doc — the traces — looks like you get large short spikes, like 2–5x baseline for 5–15 minutes. Is that consistent?
[00:38] Lena Ortiz: Yeah that's right. We have morning triage windows and event-driven surges. The tricky part is regulatory — we need all inference to be inside a VPC with no external egress, which affects how we can scale in cloud and on-prem.
[00:49] Daniel Park: Noted. We'll walk through reserved pools, burst credits, and queue-then-scale options — and how the KV cache + batching behaves under those patterns.
[00:58] [00:58] Marcus Lee: Quick Q — we use a 7B model quantized to 8-bit for cost. We see some p95 jumps when batching windows expand; curious how Redwood handles batching latency tradeoffs.
[01:10] Daniel Park: Great. We'll cover dynamic batching heuristics — batching window max, target batch size, and adaptive batching tied to latency SLO. Also how prefix (KV) cache reduces per-token compute when repeated contexts show up.

[01:40] [01:40] Daniel Park: Starting with the big picture: autoscaling knobs typically fall into three families: metric-based (GPU util, token throughput), latency-based (p95, p99), and queue-length based (request queue depth). For spiky workloads like yours, queue-length + warm capacity + burst credits is often best to avoid cold starts.
[02:04] Lena Ortiz: Can you define burst credits? Is that the same as prewarmed instances?
[02:09] Daniel Park: Related but different. A reserved pool gives you N GPUs always available — predictable throughput. Burst credits are like a bank that lets you transiently exceed reserved capacity by routing to other shared capacity or reserved overcommit for a short duration. Prewarmed instances are separate: they keep models loaded but not necessarily pinned to a customer. Bursting can be achieved by leveraging shared hosted capacity with throttles and fallbacks.
[02:32] [02:32] Ava Martinez: And for private / VPC deployments, burst behavior depends on whether customer wants local burst (additional on-prem GPUs) or remote fallback (routing back to Redwood hosted) — for strict data residency you probably need local burst hardware or a hybrid contract.

[02:54] [02:54] Marcus Lee: What about cold-starts for large models — model load time can be tens of seconds, that's a killer for spikes.
[03:00] Daniel Park: Exactly. We measure two things: model load time (cold) and token generation latency (warm). Cold starts are addressed with warm pools and incremental loading. For the 7B you mentioned, if the model is quantized and memory fits on a single V100/ A100 style GPU, model load can be 10–30s depending on I/O and init routines. With our prewarmed policy you can keep a small number of GPUs with the model loaded — either dedicated or shared — to absorb spikes. There's cost tradeoff.
[03:27] [03:27] Lena Ortiz: Are there auto-eviction policies for KV cache? We have a lot of repeated patient contexts, and the cache hit rate matters a lot.
[03:33] Daniel Park: Yes — KV cache is a major win for repeated prefixes. Our default is an LRU-style eviction with size-based thresholds, plus TTL per conversation. In VPC/private installs you can tune the cache size per serving node. Important thing: under autoscale, cache locality matters — scaling up new nodes doesn't have the cached history unless you're using a shared cache layer. So for low-latency p95 you want either sticky routing (session stickiness) or a shared KV cache with a fast in-memory store.
[04:02] [04:02] Priya Nair: One pattern we've seen work is hybrid: keep a small sticky pool per customer for recent sessions and allow overflow to a pooled burst layer that may have slightly higher latency.
[04:12] Samir Shah: That seems reasonable. Can you describe the queueing model? We've been thinking in terms of M/M/1 but unsure if it's accurate because batches create correlated service times.
[04:22] Daniel Park: Right — classic M/M/1 assumptions break when service times vary with batch size. For batched inference, it's closer to batch-service queues or M/G/k where the service time distribution is dependent on the batch. We model arrival process as Poisson-ish for baseline but heavy tailed during spikes. Practical heuristic: use queue-length thresholds to trigger scale actions and enforce a max-queue-time SLO so requests aren't queued longer than X ms. Also use admission control — small requests might be fast-path, large generation requests could go to a slower pool.
[04:56] [04:56] Marcus Lee: So admission control + adaptive batching + sticky routing = best of both worlds?
[05:01] Daniel Park: Often yes. Admission control keeps p99 guarded, adaptive batching maximizes GPU throughput, sticky routing preserves KV cache locality. You also want gradual ramping for scale-ups to avoid flapping.

[05:20] [05:20] Rina Gomez: From a security perspective: if we use shared burst capacity (hosted), how does data residency and encryption work? We need KMS integration and no-cross-tenant memory leaks, and audit logs for model access.
[05:32] Ava Martinez: Good callout. For hosted bursts, we isolate memory spaces and use encryption-in-transit and at-rest with customer KMS. Redwood also supports private endpoints/VPC peering and can provide an on-prem package. We'll share the SOC2 and VPC deployment checklist — but if policy forbids any off-prem inference you might need local burst hardware.
[05:54] [05:54] Samir Shah: Let's go into scale policies — specifically: how do we pick thresholds for queue length vs GPU util? We tried 80% GPU util but saw p95 degrade.
[06:06] Daniel Park: GPU util is a lagging indicator — it often ramps after queues form. For latency targets, queue depth and p95 latency are better early-warning signals. A combined policy works best: if queue depth > Q and p95 > target, spin up N nodes; if GPU util > 85% for sustained window, add capacity for throughput. Also implement cooldown periods; don't immediately spin down until token backlog clears.
[06:31] [06:31] Ethan Zhou: Another lever: model quantization. Moving 8-bit to 4-bit can double effective capacity but might slightly alter outputs. We can recommend specific quant profiles per workload. The Optimize team has a library of quantization calibrations and regression tests.
[06:48] Marcus Lee: We did an internal A/B — 4-bit gave ~1.9x throughput improvements and 5–7% quality delta in some prompt classes, so maybe use 4-bit for lower-criticality routes. How would Redwood manage multiple quantized variants?
[06:59] Daniel Park: We support model variants with a routing policy: route to high-precision model for sensitive flows, low-precision for bulk. You can use canary and A/B via console. Also fallback policies: if a lower precision variant fails, automatically route to a reserved high-precision node.

[07:20] [07:20] Lena Ortiz: About reserved GPUs: how many should we reserve? We don't want to pay for 100% headroom.
[07:27] Daniel Park: Reserve enough to cover a normal burst baseline: for example, if your 95th percentile peak needs 10 GPUs and baseline is 4, maybe reserve 6 and use burst credits for the rest. We'll run a sizing model — which is why the 7-day traces help. We'll put a cost-sensitivity table: reserved vs on-demand vs burst.
[07:44] Ava Martinez: We'll include different scenarios: aggressive reserve (higher cost, low risk), conservative reserve + larger burst window (lower cost, more reliance on shared capacity), and fully private with on-prem burst (higher Ops).

[08:02] [08:02] Samir Shah: Question — how do we handle preemption if using shared cloud GPUs? We can't have important inference preempted mid‑request.
[08:10] Daniel Park: Preemption is handled at the scheduling layer: Redwood pins in-flight requests and avoids preemption until request stream drains for that GPU. For hosted environments we use instance types that support low preemption or we buffer requests and move them safely. For guaranteed workloads you want dedicated GPUs.
[08:27] [08:27] Marcus Lee: Is there visibility into per-token cost and per-route latency so we can tune routing?
[08:33] Priya Nair: Yes — console exposes token-level cost, p50/p95/p99 by route and model variant, and breakdown by batching efficiency and KV cache hit rate. We'll show a sample later.

[08:50] [08:50] Lena Ortiz: One more on batching — when you say adaptive batching, what's the typical max latency window? We tried 100ms and it was ok, sometimes it grew to 400ms during spikes.
[08:59] Daniel Park: Typical windows are 20–100ms for low-latency apps. For higher throughput you can allow up to 200ms. The adaptive policy tries to cap additional batching if p95 approaches SLO. Also note that batch size increases service time non-linearly; very large batches can increase p99 due to head-of-line blocking.

[09:20] [09:20] Samir Shah: Can Redwood simulate our traffic to estimate costs?
[09:24] Ava Martinez: Yes — we can run synthetic replay in our staging cluster or give you a containerized benchmark harness to run locally (for VPC). We typically ask for a 24‑72 hour trace for accurate sim.
[09:36] Daniel Park: We'll also run mixed-workload sims: short-chat requests intermixed with long-gen requests to see the queueing coupling. That will inform the admission control rules.

[10:00] [10:00] Marcus Lee: A small nit — you mentioned shared KV caches might leak? We can't have cross-customer state.
[10:06] Daniel Park: No cross-customer leakage — shared layer is multi-tenant in the sense of resources but encrypted and logically partitioned. But sticky routing + local cache avoids network roundtrips and keeps latency lower.

[10:24] [10:24] Rina Gomez: And the audit logs — we need per-request logs (no PII) and key rotation compliance.
[10:31] Ava Martinez: We'll include the retention, redaction options, and KMS key rotation docs.

[10:40] [10:40] Recap & Proposed Runbook:
- Collect 7-day traces (Samir)
- Redwood to run a 24-hour baseline replay in staging with three scenarios: reserve-heavy, reserve-light + burst, and hybrid prewarm + admission control
- SE to produce recommended GPU mix, reserved pool size, burst credit policy, and quant profiles
- Security to review VPC flow and SOC2 docs

[10:58] [10:58] Ava Martinez: Any final questions?
[11:02] Lena Ortiz: One last thing — when doing scale down, what's typical cooldown? We saw flapping because scale-down happened too quickly after short drop.
[11:09] Daniel Park: Use a multi-window cooldown: don't scale down until your token backlog is zero and util is below threshold for a 5–10 minute window. We also use predictive cooldowns based on time-of-day patterns.
[11:21] Samir Shah: Sounds good, thanks. We'll get the traces over.
[11:24] Ava Martinez: Great — we'll send the spreadsheet and draft runbook after this call, and Daniel will get the GPU recommendations. Thanks everyone.

[11:30] (call ends)
